introduction-the-illusion-of-a-single-co.core: Replication keeps multiple copies for availability and performance, but clients would ideally see a single, up-to-date copy. Consistency models define what clients may observe when reading replicated data: from linearizability (looks like one copy in real time) through sequential and causal consistency to eventual consistency. Stronger models cost latency and availability (CAP/PACELC).

first_principles.problem: A user updates their profile, refreshes and sees the old version, and support tickets pile up.
truths: Applications differ in what they tolerate.

analogy.title: Copies of a shared document
analogy.story: Ideally everyone sees the latest edit instantly; in practice some copies are a few seconds behind.
analogy.breaks: Documents sync visibly; replicas lag invisibly.

check.q: What does PACELC add to CAP?
check.a: Even without partitions (Else), systems trade Latency against Consistency.

strong-consistency-linearizability.core: Linearizability means every operation appears to take effect atomically at a single point between its start and end, consistent with real-time order: once a write completes, all later reads see it (or something newer). It's what 'behaves like a single copy' means, and it's needed for locks, leader election, uniqueness constraints and balances. It requires coordination (consensus, quorum reads) and suffers during partitions.

first_principles.problem: Two users register the same username because each replica checked uniqueness independently.
truths: Real-time order matters for some invariants.
derivation: Use **quorum reads/writes** or **leader reads with leases**.

analogy.title: A single ledger book on one desk
analogy.story: Everyone writes and reads the same physical book, so nobody ever sees an outdated page.
analogy.breaks: One book can only serve one person at a time; linearizable systems still serve many clients concurrently.

example.title: Unique username
flow: Conditional put 'username:ada' with create-if-absent in etcd

check.q: What does linearizability guarantee after a write completes?
check.a: Every subsequent read (by anyone) returns that value or a newer one.

sequential-consistency-order-matters-tim.core: Sequential consistency requires that all processes see operations in the same total order, consistent with each process's own program order, but not necessarily matching real time. A write might become visible 'late' as long as everyone agrees on the order. It's weaker than linearizability and historically relevant to multiprocessor memory models.

first_principles.problem: Engineers confuse 'everyone sees the same order' with 'everyone sees the latest value immediately'.
truths: Agreement on order differs from real-time recency.
Hardware memory models use such definitions.
derivation: Relevant to **CPU memory models** and some replicated logs.

analogy.title: A sports replay everyone watches in the same order, delayed
analogy.story: All viewers see goals in the same sequence, though some streams are behind live.
analogy.breaks: Viewers notice delays vs live; processes can't tell how far behind real time they are.

example.title: Allowed history
flow: Allowed under sequential (order: P2 read, then write)

check.q: What's the key difference between sequential consistency and linearizability?
check.a: Sequential consistency doesn't require the global order to respect real-time ordering of non-overlapping operations.

eventual-consistency-the-optimists-choic.core: Eventual consistency only promises that if writes stop, all replicas will converge to the same value. Reads may return stale data in the meantime, and concurrent writes need conflict resolution (last-write-wins, vector clocks with merges, CRDTs). It maximises availability and low latency and suits DNS, caches, counters and social feeds.

first_principles.problem: A globally distributed shopping cart must accept writes in every region even during partitions.
truths: Coordination-free writes are fast and available.
derivation: Resolve conflicts with **LWW, merges or CRDTs**.

analogy.title: News spreading by word of mouth
analogy.story: Eventually everyone hears, though some hear later or briefly hear an outdated version.
analogy.breaks: Rumours can mutate; replicas converge to a deterministic result if conflicts are resolved correctly.

example.title: Dynamo-style cart
flow: Partition: EU and US replicas both accept cart edits

check.a: That replicas converge to the same value if no new updates are made.

causal-consistency-the-middle-ground.core: Causal consistency guarantees that causally related operations are seen by everyone in the same order (a reply is never seen before the post it answers), while concurrent operations may be seen in different orders. It's the strongest model that remains available during partitions and is implemented with dependency tracking or vector clocks (e.g. COPS, MongoDB causal sessions).

first_principles.problem: Users see replies to comments that don't appear yet, because the reply replicated faster than the original.
truths: Tracking dependencies is cheaper than global order.

analogy.title: Email threads
analogy.story: You'll never see a reply before the email it replies to, but unrelated emails can arrive in any order.
analogy.breaks: Email clients show threads visually; replicas must buffer effects until causes arrive.

example.title: Comment then reply
flow: Bob reads C1, replies R1 (US) with dependency on C1
Asia replica receives R1 first → waits for C1

check.q: Why is causal consistency attractive for geo-distributed apps?
check.a: It preserves intuitive cause-effect order while remaining available during partitions.

client-centric-consistency-models.core: Client-centric (session) guarantees give each user a sensible view even on weakly consistent systems: read-your-writes (you see your own updates), monotonic reads (you never see older data after newer), monotonic writes (your writes apply in order) and writes-follow-reads (your write after reading X is ordered after X). They're implemented with sticky routing, session tokens or version vectors.

first_principles.problem: A user posts a comment, refreshes and it's gone because the read hit a lagging replica.
truths: Users notice their own changes most.
Going back in time feels broken.
derivation: **Read-your-writes**: route to leader or wait for session version.
**Monotonic reads**: stick to a replica or track a version.
Carry **session tokens** (e.g. Cosmos DB, MongoDB causal sessions).
Use **sticky load balancing** as a simple approach.

analogy.title: A personal assistant who remembers what you just told them
analogy.story: Even if the office files are behind, they won't contradict what you said a minute ago.
analogy.breaks: Assistants remember everything; session guarantees cover only that client's view, not others'.

example.title: Session token
flow: Client sends token with next read
Replica waits until it has v ≥ 1042 (or forwards)
User always sees their own comment

check.a: A client always sees its own previous writes in subsequent reads.
